about: Document-type search over real scanned office pages. Dataset: RVL-CDIP with Amazon Textract OCR, Hugging Face stefan-hf/rvlcdip-redact (https://huggingface.co/datasets/stefan-hf/rvlcdip-redact), config textract_redact, split test, revision a1f0f0406f9c146340713f03f06898ccfff4c073. Licence: other: the dataset card applies the terms of the Legacy Tobacco Document Library / IIT-CDIP, https://www.industrydocuments.ucsf.edu/help/copyright/. Attribution: OCR text of RVL-CDIP test pages (A. W. Harley, A. Ufkes, K. G. Derpanis, ICDAR 2015), a subset of IIT-CDIP (D. Lewis et al., SIGIR 2006) drawn from the Legacy Tobacco Document Library, UCSF Industry Documents Library; Amazon Textract OCR and corrected labels from stefan-hf/rvlcdip-redact (S. Larson et al., DocEng 2025). Corpus: 195 pages, 13 per class for 15 of the 16 classes, sampled with seed 20261120 from 800 rows in seeded 100-row blocks of the test split; a page qualifies when its original and corrected labels agree, its OCR text has at least 30 words and at most 5000 characters. 'file folder' is left out: none of its pages in the sample has 30 words. Content is the OCR text as is (noisy); titles are neutral ('Scan 0001'); pages are spread over 5 placeholder clients. Labels: class queries take relevance from the RVL-CDIP labels; purpose queries from this written mapping: 'someone's work history' -> resume; 'price list or bill' -> invoice + budget; 'planned spending' -> budget; 'internal office note' -> memo; 'promotional material for a product' -> advertisement; 'technical requirements for a product' -> specification; 'press coverage' -> news article; 'research findings' -> scientific report + scientific publication; acceptable pages and negative queries come from a whole-word string check of the query words (fixed -s/-es/-ed/-d/-ing forms); detail strings occur in exactly one page. Built by research/datasets/build/ds_rvlcdip_types.py from research/datasets/raw/rvlcdip/. Pages per class: advertisement 13, budget 13, email 13, form 13, handwritten 13, invoice 13, letter 13, memo 13, news article 13, presentation 13, questionnaire 13, resume 13, scientific publication 13, scientific report 13, specification 13.

Dear U.S. Representative Gejdensen:
The use of tobacco by children has reached epidemic numbers in our country. These numbers are
even more alarming/when we realize that these children WETE targeted in marketing strategies by the
tobacco industry. The time is now to establish a tough national tobacco policy.
While we applaud recent efforts by the President and Congress for initiatives and proposals
designed to cortail teen smoking, we urge you to support the June 20th agreement between the Attorneys
General and the tobacco industry. This agreement establishes nationwide restrictions on access to tobacco
products, eliminates youth targeted advertising, sets specific targets for ending the teen smoking problem
and requires Industry-funded programs for health research, education and cessation programs. This
agreement provides the framework for the most sweeping teen smoking prevention legislation ever
adopted.
Recent concessions by the tobacco industry. including the release of teen marketing efforts and
proposals to restrict tobacco use among young people, deserve to be recognized and commended
However, we must make sure that these strategies and the problem of teen smoking are curtailed once and
for all. The June 20, 1997 agreement would end such marketing and provide substantial dollars to aid
states in the resultant health care and prevention costs.
We have passed strict laws in Connecticut to address the teen smoking problem, however,
without federal restrictions on advertising and licensing, these laws will have little impact the national
crisis. We look forward to working with you in any way we can to help curb the underage use of tobacco.

PROJECT DESCRIPTION
TITLE: Structure-Function Studies of Tubulin: The Roles of Conserved Cysteine
Residues and The Non-exchangeable GTP Site.
INTRODUCTION
Tubulin is an essential cellular protein in eukaryotes, playing a role in
chromosome and other types of cellular movement Progress in determining the
structure of tubulin has been very slow, and in its absence, problems related to
assigning function to specific regions of the protein are best studied using a
mutagenesis approach. have just finished a sabbatical year in the laboratory of Dr.
Kevin Farrell at the University of California, Santa Barbara, where I learned the
techniques and methodologies used to mutagenize yeast tubulin. For the most part,
my studies of tubulin and microtubules have had a chemical orientation, and I now
plan to add this approach to my laboratory at the University of Kansas. It will be used to
study the role of nucleotides in microtubule assembly and stability and to address
questions concerning the function of specific amino acid residues and regions of the
protein molecule. Abbreviated background and experimental sections are presented
below. Because of space limitations references have been omitted.
OVERALL GOALS AND SPECIFIC AIMS
The overall goal of this study is to identify amino acid residues in tubulin that are
hypothesized to be involved in GTP binding and/or hydrolysis and others that may be
involved in dimer-dimer interactions during microtubule assembly. In this proposal we
shall concentrate on the following aims.
1. To mutagenize residues in a-tubulin that may be involved in nucleotide
binding.
2. To change conserved cysteine residues to alanines.
3. To study the effects of these mutations on the biochemical properties of yeast
tubulin and on certain cellular microtubule-dependent processes.
BACKGROUND AND SIGNIFICANCE
GTP binding sites, GTPase activity, and microtubule stability.
Microtubules (MTs) are essential elements in several cellular processes,
including chromosome movement and intracellular transport. Cytoplasmic and mitotic
MTs are dynamic structures, meaning that in a population of MTs, individual MTs
elongate or shorten while the total mass of MTs remains constant, i.e. at steady state.
This behavior is thought to be a necessary property as the MTs search for their targets,
e.g. kinetochores. It is also thought to be involved in the movement of chromosomes
during mitosis. This dynamic nature of MTs is undoubtedly under cellular control as
mitotic MTs grow and shorten at rates which are 20- to 100-fold higher than
cytoplasmic MTs.
The protein component of MTs is tubulin, a heterodimeric molecule with two
guanine nucleotide binding sites, an exchangeable site (E-site) on the B-subunit and a
non-exchangeable site (N-site) on the a-subunit. The N-site is always occupied by
GTP while the E-site is occupied by GTP or GDP. During the addition of a tubulin dimer
to the end of a growing MT, GTP at the E-site undergoes hydrolysis to GDP and Pi.
One model for dimer addition to a MT proposes that an incoming tubulin molecule
induces the hydrolysis of the GTP in the former terminal dimer. A consequence of this
model is that a MT is capped at the ends by tubulin-GTP molecules.

HEADLINE: Target marketing lights smoky fire
BYLINE: By Janet Cawley, Chicago Tribune
DATELINE: WASHINGTON
BODY:
Target marketing - a standard practice for selling anything from cleansers to
Cadillacs - has touched off a furor in the already highly charged world of
cigarette selling and smoking.
The catalyst for the most recent skirmish in the longstanding battle between
smokers and nonsmokers was the disclosure earlier this year that R.J. Reynolds
Tobacco Co. planned to market a new brand of cigarettes, Uptown, targeted at
blacks.
This was followed several weeks later by the revelation that Reynolds had at
least considered a proposal to aim another brand, called Dakota, at
18-to-20-year-old women with high school educations who aspired to marry early
and who enjoyed such activities as tractor pulls and drag races.
Suddenly the somewhat prosaic concept of target marketing had been
transformed into what the antismokers, at least, consider no less than a matter
of life and death.
"They are targeting communities for death and destruction," said Dr. Michele
Bloch of the Women Vs. Smoking Network. "They have a legal right to target, but
the community has a legal right to 'just say no. , "
But the cigarette companies say they're only doing what's logical and
accepted for any product.
"Any product you market, by the simple fact it's on the market, is going to
be targeted," said David Fishel, a spokesman for Reynolds. "It's going to fall
into demographic segments."
The war of words hit the boiling point when the nation's top health official,
Dr. Louis Sullivan, emerged from the low-profile cocoon of his first year in
President Bush's Cabinet to condemn the campaigns.
Sullivan, secretary of health and human services, called the Uptown campaign
"slick and sinster" and charged it with "promoting a culture of cancer."
At stake here are a lot of things, not the least of which is money.

PHILIP MORRIS U.S.A. SAYS IT WILL PREVAIL AGAINST
INDIANA AG'S MEDICAID SUIT
NEW YORK, February 19, 1997 - Philip Morris U.S.A. will vigorously defend this
politically motivated, copycat lawsuit, and the company firmly believes it will ultimately
prevail.
By bringing this ill-advised case, Indiana's Attorney General is mimicking the
actions of several other state attorneys general. He is, to the detriment of Indiana's
citizens, following in the footsteps of a self-interested mix of politicians and a roving
band of plaintiffs' contingency fee lawyers who believe they can disregard established
product liability law and use the courts to legislate public policy on tobacco and become
richer.
Highlighting the purely political and legally baseless nature of the suit is its
timing. Indiana has filed in the wake of a West Virginia court's decision to dismiss 11 of
14 claims of that state's lawsuit against the industry.
"It is unfortunate that the state's most senior legal officer has ignored the fact
that the state has no viable legal basis upon which to sue cigarette manufacturers," said
Gregory G. Little, senior assistant general counsel for Philip Morris. "We believe it is
regrettable that a duly elected official feels so little constraint by law or fact that he
willingly jumps on what is perceived by some to be the politically correct bandwagon of
tobacco litigation."
"At the same time, law-abiding manufacturers and businesses across the state
must now be deeply concerned that they, too, may be the target of such lawsuits, no
matter how meritless," added Little.
Philip Morris believes that the state will lose and in the end, it will be the
taxpayers of Indiana who will pay the price for Attorney General Modisett's blatant
political grandstanding.

(1) Improved Parliament
Evaluation of a new Parliament 85 model. incorporating
a 25 mm filter (20 mm CA/5 mm recess) and a CFF Parliament
blend with flavor compensation, versus production Parliament
by a Richmond Placement Panel showed the experimental cigaret
to be significantly less harsh or strong. The smokers also
tended to judge the current Parliament as more bitter and the
experimental model as weaker. Parliament smokers on the panel
found no significant differences between the two cigarets.
HTI testing of this cigaret as well as an 80 mm model with
the same filter and blend versus production controls was
initiated.
(2) 85 mm Slim Cigaret
Development of an 85 mm slim cigaret having tar
delivery, puff count, and taste characteristics, as judged
by the Flavor Development Group, similar to a Marlboro 85
was completed. Evaluation by a Richmond Placement panel
is being implemented. Larger scale mailout testing will be
scheduled if results of the local testing are favorable.
(3) Modified Project Premium
POL mailout testing of a modified Project Premium
prototype having a higher puff delivery profile and a
slightly lower puff count than its equal delivery Project
Premium control (16 mg tar delivery) indicated the cigarets
were equally preferred by the total panel. The altered
delivery profile was achieved with a less porous, faster
burn cigaret paper than that used on the control. The
modified version was more acceptable to younger smokers,
females, and light smokers while the control was preferred
by older smokers.

Subject:
"Guidelines for Smoking Control" - analysis and impact
Analysis
The "Guidelines for Smoking Control" is a 134 page document
which describes a variety of programs for controlling smoking.
The manual was written by Messrs. Nigel Gray and Michael Daube
under the auspices of the International Union Against Cancer
(UICC)
The UICC is an international organization whose general
mandate is to "achieve the eventual prevention and cure of
cancer" Its membership consists of 188 organizations represent-
ing 77 countries. It has an operating budget of approximately
U.S. $2,000,000.
Through its alliance with the World Health Organization,
The International Agency for Research on Cancer and other
groups, the UICC has been a leader in developing smoking
control strategies and programs worldwide. It is responsible
also for publication of a number of periodicals and working
papers covering a broad spectrum of cancer related issues.
The UICC has organized a number of symposia on smoking
and health. In October 1980, three smoking control symposia
were conducted in South America which were attended by local
national cancer societies and other UICC affiliated organiza-
tions. The "Guidelines for Somking Control" was prepared as
a result of an earlier symposium held in Paris during April, 1980.
The Guidelines has ten chapters and four appendices.
Chapters one through five set forth the rationales behind
smoking control programs. Included in these sections are
the UICC's policy objectives, an outline of the scientific
evidence supporting the anti-smoking movement's allegations
and the broad strategies to be applied toward the control of
smoking worldwide.

C.C. Benz, S.B. lyer, H.S. Asgari, S.A. Matlin, F.A. Aronson, and A Barchowsky
Cancer Research Institute University of California, San Francisco, CA 94143 and
Clinical Pharmacology, Thomas Jefferson University, Philadelphia, PA 19107
Abstract Isomers (-.+) of the antitumor agent gossypol (G) were studied for their ability to reduce tumor
ATP and blood flow in rats bearing subcutaneously implanted pancreatic tumors. A 50% reduction in
tumor ATP/PI within Ih of a single injection of -G was associated with a 60% decline in tumor blood flow.
To determine if these changes in tumor physiology could be due to a direct drug effect on tumor
endothelium G isomers were compared for their ability to alter protein (251-BSA) permeability and
metabolic (32P) labelling of cultured endothelial cells. Treatments for in produced no endothelial cell
leakage. but 24h exposures to either -G(SuM) or +G(50uM) produced complete permeability of the
monolayers to 1251-BSA In contrast, 0.5-1.0h exposures to -G(4uM) or +G(10um) produced 2 to 3-fold
increases in phosphorylated 27kDa heat-shock protein, hsp-27. Hsp-27 phosphoprotein isoforms were
differentially labelled following -G and +G exposures with the phosphorylation profile of -G appearing
most similar to that of oxyradical producing agents known to induce hsp-27 and injure endothelial cells.
We postulate that the tumor ischemic effects of -G are mediated by endothelial response to oxyradical
production in a mechanism similar to that of tissue ischemia-reperfusion injury
INTRODUCTION
Gossypol (G) is a plant-derived binaphthol with antiproliterative activity against epithelial carcinomas
of breast, ovarian, colon and pancreatic origin (1). G has antitumor properties similar to those of
lipophilic antimitochondrial agents (like rhodamine and platinum-modamine). and we have demonstrated
that phosphorus magnetic resonance spectroscopy (31P-MRS) provides a rapid means of noninvasively
monitoring tumors for the uncoupling ATPase effects of such antimilochondrial agents (2-5). G is also a
potent inhibitor of various non-mitochondrial enzymes such as calmodulin (CaM) stimulated cyclic
nucleotide phosphodiesterase and protein kinase C (PKC), raising the question of whether the
antitumor properties of G are due to its andimilochondrial or enzyme inhibitory mechanisms (1). Of the
two naturally occuring G enantiomers (- +) studied in vitro, -G produces 10-fold greater antiproliferative
and antimitochondrial effects while both isomers are equally potent inhibitors of CaM and PKC (1). At
present little is known about the in vivo effects of these two isomers on tumor bioenergetics and
physiology. Modest growth inhibiting doses of some antimitochondrial agents produce prominent in
vivo reductions in tumor ATP levels measured by 31P-MRS as early as 60 min after intraperitoneal (ip)
drug injection (4.5). Studies with the metabolic inhibitor flavorie acetic acid (FAA) indicate that early
reductions in tumor ATP are associated with a concomitant decline in tumor blood flow, as monitored by
deuterium spectroscopy (6). This finding prompted our analysis of G effects on tumor ATP and blood
flow as well as a comparison of G enantiomer effects on cultured endothelial cells.
METHODS
Drugs Cells and Assays

(Washington, DC) - A vast majority of Americans believe the federal Food and Drug
Administration (FDA) is not an efficient agency and that its regulations and procedures
result in lost lives and higher medical costs, according to a new national survey
commissioned by Citizens for a Sound Economy (CSE) Foundation, a nonpartisan, nonprofit
research and education organization formed in 1984 to study and develop market-based
solutions to public policy problems.
Paul Beckner, president of CSE Foundation, says the results of the survey will bolster
the need for reforming the FDA. "When people learn that in Canada a medical device is
approved for use in less than ninety days, but here in the U.S. it will take our government
nearly a decade to do the same, they see a problem. When they learn that every year tens of
thousands of Americans die while the FDA delays approval of drugs readily available in
Europe, they see a problem. And when they learn that while the media can tell you aspirin
could help prevent a second heart attack, the aspirin's maker can't because FDA rules say
they can't, they see a problem. In fact, on a series of questions that address these issues, no
fewer than two out of every three voters agree that current FDA regulations and procedures
result in lost lives and higher medical costs for American consumers."
Sixty-five percent of the survey's respondents disagreed with the statement that the
FDA "is quick and efficient" and - because of its lengthy, costly procedures - actually

higher number - 68 percent - agreed that "the additional years it takes for the FDA to
approve products costs lives by forcing people, including those with incurable diseases, to go

The drug lag: An update of new drug
introductions in the United States
and in the United Kingdom, 1977
through 1987
This report updates previous studies that documented the existence of a significant lag between new drug
introductions in the United Kingdom and in the United States. During the 11-year period from 1977
through 1987, the United Kingdom led the United States in the number of first introductions of new
drugs (114 versus 41), in average lead time for murually available drugs (60.7 versus 28.9 months). and
in the number of exclusively available drugs (70 versus 54). Analysis by therapeutic ategory indicated large
United Kingdom leads in the introduction of respiratory (6.1 years), cardiovascular (3.2 years), central
nervous system (3.2 years), and anti-cancer (2.9 years) agents, and shorter leads for anestheric and analgesic
(2.0 years), gastrointestical (2.0 years), endocrine (1.4 years), and anti-infective (0.8 years) agents. A
comparison of the S-year period from 1983 through 1987 with the previous S-year period (1978 through
1982) showed no change in the length of the lag time (1.9 years for each period). These results indicate
that the United States continues to lag behind the United Kingdom in the availability of new drugs.
